mainKeyword: best ceramic space heater for rv
guideTitle: Best Ceramic Space Heaters for RVs (2026)
metaTitle: Best Ceramic Space Heaters for RVs 2026
metaDescription: Six PTC ceramic space heaters for RVs compared by wattage, noise, size and safety shutoffs, with picks for 30 amp rigs and tight camper floors.
expertTake: The DREO Atom One is the best ceramic heater for most RVs thanks to its quiet motor and digital thermostat, and the Amazon Basics oscillating unit is the value pick. Owners who already have a working furnace and only need a morning boost can skip anything over 900 watts.
introParagraphs: Ceramic heaters use a PTC element, a ceramic stone whose electrical resistance climbs as it warms. That property caps its own temperature, so the element cannot run away the way a bare coil can. A fan blows room air across it and you feel warmth within seconds.

In an RV that quick, self-limiting behavior is the appeal. Cabins are small and well sealed, so a modest unit raises the temperature fast. The real limits are the electrical budget on a 30 amp pedestal and the fan noise next to your bed.

products.name: DREO Atom One 1500W Oscillating Ceramic Heater
products.description:
DREO's Atom One drives a 1500 watt PTC ceramic element with a brushless DC fan motor and nine curved blades. That motor choice is the real engineering win, because brushless fans run smoother and more quietly than the brushed motors in cheaper units. The oscillating head sweeps 70 degrees, which spreads warmth across a typical RV living area instead of drilling one spot.

A digital thermostat holds the cabin to a set temperature by cycling the element, so average draw drops once the space is warm. Next to the Lasko tower in this roundup it is quieter and more compact, though the Lasko offers a taller reach. The remote is handy when the heater sits across the room from your bed.

On a 30 amp RV circuit, 1500 watts is about 12.5 amps, so you must watch what else is running. Dust the intake grille each month, because lint is the main thing that makes a ceramic fan noisier over time. ETL-listed tip-over and overheat protection is standard and worth confirming on arrival.
products.bestFor: Most RV owners who want a quiet, controllable main heater.

ETL-listed tip-over and overheat shutoffs
cons: At 1500W it takes a big slice of a 30 amp circuit
Oscillating head adds a moving part to maintain

products.name: Amazon Basics Oscillating Ceramic Heater 1500W/900W
products.description:
Amazon Basics offers the plainest version of the idea: a ceramic element, three switch positions and a 45 degree oscillation sweep. The 900 watt low setting is the useful part for RVs, because it draws roughly 7.5 amps and leaves headroom on a shared circuit. Fan-only mode doubles as a cabin air mover in summer.

It weighs about three pounds and measures 7.5 by 6.3 by 9.5 inches, so it tucks onto a shelf or the floor of a galley without taking space. Against the DREO Atom One it has no digital thermostat, so you manage the temperature by switching it on and off. That makes it a better fit for short bursts than for overnight use.

Small and light means a lower center of gravity than a tower, which helps stability in a moving rig. Store it in a bin during travel and wipe the grille with a dry cloth. Treat the cord as part of the build, and replace the unit if the plug ever runs warm.

products.name: Amazon Basics Ceramic Heater 1500W with Thermostat
products.description:
This is the fixed-head sibling of the oscillating unit, trading the sweep for a thermostat dial on the same compact body. With no oscillation motor there is one less part to wear out, which matters when a heater rattles around in storage. Thermostat control cycles the element once the cabin reaches your setting.

The same 1500, 900 and fan-only choices apply, so you can drop to 900 watts to share a 30 amp circuit. Next to the oscillating model, it concentrates heat in one direction, which suits a bedside or desk spot. It lacks the room-wide spread of the DREO Atom One, but the footprint stays smaller.

A mechanical dial thermostat is less accurate than a digital one, so expect a few degrees of swing. Keep the front grille free of lint and never cover it with a blanket. If the cord or plug gets hot, stop using it immediately.

products.name: BLACK+DECKER BHDC201 Personal Ceramic Heater 1500W
products.description:
BLACK+DECKER's BHDC201 is a personal-size ceramic heater with fan-only, 750 watt and 1500 watt settings. Its 750 watt step sits lower than most competitors' 900 watt step, which makes it the gentlest option for a shared RV circuit. A power-on indicator tells you at a glance that it is running.

It works best as a spot heater for a desk, a galley counter or a dinette, rather than as the main heat source. Next to the 500 watt ASNUG it moves more air and heat, but it is noisier and larger. The brand name carries a service network that matters if you need a replacement.

The fan is the loudest part, so use the 750 watt step overnight if you can tolerate the cooler air. Rest it on a hard, flat surface and away from curtains. Vacuum the intake slots seasonally to keep air moving.

products.name: ASNUG 500W Mini PTC Ceramic Heater
products.description:
ASNUG's 500 watt mini heater is a palm-sized PTC unit that draws about 4 amps. It is the lowest draw in this roundup, so it can run alongside an air conditioner or a microwave on a tight 30 amp rig. The listing advertises a silent mode and flame-retardant housing.

Small output means small reach: it warms a lap, a desk or a bathroom corner, not a whole trailer. Think of it as a supplement for a bunk, a closet-sized bedroom or a pet area. Against the 1500 watt picks, it will not keep up with cold weather by itself.

Its tiny footprint is easy to stow in a drawer. Clean the intake with a dry brush, and do not leave it running unattended in a closed space. Replace it if the plug feels warm to the touch.

products.name: Lasko 23 inch Oscillating Ceramic Tower Heater
products.description:
Lasko's tower puts a long 1500 watt ceramic element in a tall, narrow cabinet and quotes 5,118 BTU. The elongated element heats quickly, and the oscillating head throws warmth across the room. A thermostat and remote complete the package.

Tall and slim suits a corner of the RV where floor space is limited. Beside the compact Amazon Basics units, it covers more area but stands higher, so it tips over more easily on a moving or uneven floor. Tower units generally deserve extra care in a rig that bounces over roads.

Secure it in transit and never run it while driving. Wipe dust from the front grille and check the rear filter if present. If your RV circuit is already busy, the 1500 watt draw is still about 12.5 amps.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A 1500 watt heater draws about 12.5 amps at 120 volts, which is a big share of a 30 amp RV service. On the same circuit as an air conditioner or a microwave it will trip a breaker. The ASNUG at 500 watts draws about 4 amps, and the Amazon Basics units drop to 900 watts. Know your circuit before you pick.

A thermostat cycles the element so it only draws full power when needed. The DREO Atom One and Lasko both have one, and the non-oscillating Amazon Basics has a dial. Without one, such as on the oscillating Amazon Basics, you switch it by hand. Digital controls hold the cabin temperature more tightly than a dial.

The fan is the noisy part of a ceramic heater, since the element itself is silent. The DREO's brushless motor is built to run quieter than the brushed motors in basic units. Maker noise figures are claims, so favor a brushless design if you sleep within a few feet of it.

RV floors flex and slope, and a heater can slide on a trip. Tip-over switches cut power if the unit falls, and overheat cutoffs protect the element. All six picks list these, but confirm they are present on your unit. Look for ETL or UL listing marks.

Cabin storage is limited, and a heater has to travel with you. The ASNUG measures 6.1 by 5.75 by 2.87 inches, while the Lasko stands 23 inches tall. Pick a size you can secure in transit. Tall towers need a strap or a bin.

Oscillation does not add output, it only changes where the air goes. The DREO sweeps 70 degrees and the Amazon Basics sweeps 45. In a long, narrow RV that spread is useful, while in a small bedroom it hardly matters.

howWeEvaluated.title: Electrical draw
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared each heater's wattage steps against a 30 amp RV circuit. The 500W ASNUG and 750W BLACK+DECKER step score well for sharing, while 1500W models need dedicated headroom. This is based on the spec sheet.

howWeEvaluated.title: Noise and motor type
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for brushless motors and silent modes, then weighed owner feedback patterns on fan noise. Maker decibel figures were treated as claims. The DREO scored highest for bedroom use.

howWeEvaluated.title: Control and thermostat
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked for digital thermostats, dials, remotes and fixed switches. Digital control with a remote beats a manual switch for overnight use. Units without a thermostat were scored lower for unattended heating.

howWeEvaluated.title: Size and stability
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared footprint and shape. Compact units like the ASNUG and Amazon Basics stay stable, while the 23 inch Lasko tower needs more care on a moving floor. Stowage also counted.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety features
howWeEvaluated.description: We confirmed each listing mentions tip-over and overheat protection. Listings with ETL or UL marks gained credit. We did not assume features that were not stated.

faq.q: Is a ceramic heater better than an oil-filled one for an RV?
faq.a: Ceramic units warm up in seconds and are light, which suits small cabins. Oil-filled radiators are quieter but heavy and slow. For a moving rig, ceramic is usually easier to stow.

faq.q: How much does it cost to run?
faq.a: One hour at 1500 watts uses 1.5 kilowatt-hours. A thermostat reduces the average draw once the space is warm, so actual use is lower.

faq.q: Will a ceramic heater trip my RV breaker?
faq.a: It can if you run it with an air conditioner or microwave on the same 30 amp supply. At 1500 watts it draws about 12.5 amps. Use a 900 watt or lower setting to share.

faq.q: Does a higher wattage heat faster?
faq.a: Yes, since heat output scales with watts. But all 1500 watt resistance heaters make about the same BTU, so differences come from airflow and control.

faq.q: Can I leave it on overnight?
faq.a: Use a unit with tip-over and overheat shutoffs and a thermostat, and keep three feet of clearance from bedding. Never leave any heater running when you leave the RV.

faq.q: Do I need an extension cord?
faq.a: Plug directly into the wall outlet or the pedestal receptacle. Extension cords and power strips can overheat at heater loads, and a thin cord is the usual culprit when a plug runs warm.
